wrong: Secure housing for inmates awaiting trial
Detainees awaiting trial are held in jails. Halfway houses serve offenders who are re-entering the community.
Temporary shelter for victims of abuse
That describes a crisis or women's shelter. Halfway houses house offenders returning to society.
Diagnostic units for newly committed inmates
New inmates go to the reception and diagnostic center. Halfway houses come at the end of the sentence, before full release.
Prepare inmates for their release
Pre-release programs do that near the end of the sentence. The RDC handles inmates at the start, on admission.
Hold inmates under disciplinary penalty
That is disciplinary segregation. The RDC studies and classifies newly committed inmates.
Process visitors and inmate mail
Visitation and mail are handled by custodial staff. The RDC exists to assess and classify new inmates.
Religion, hometown, and family background
These are not classification criteria; classifying by religion or origin would be discriminatory. Classification looks at the offense, sentence, conduct and risk.
Age, gender, and educational attainment only
These may affect housing or programs, but classification rests on the crime, sentence, behavior and security risk.
Physical strength and work skills
Skills may matter for work assignments, not for classification, which weighs the crime, sentence, behavior and risk.
For inmates with short sentences
Short sentences usually point to minimum security. Maximum security is for the most dangerous inmates.
For inmates nearing their release
Inmates close to release are usually moved down to minimum security. Maximum security is for the highest-risk inmates.
For first-time offenders
Being a first offender does not make an inmate high-risk. Maximum security is for the most dangerous inmates.
For high-risk inmates
High-risk inmates go to maximum security. Minimum security is for low-risk inmates.
For inmates serving life terms
Inmates serving life terms are classified maximum security, not minimum.
For newly arrived inmates
New arrivals first go through reception and diagnosis before any security level is assigned.
Age, height, and physical build
Physical traits do not decide the security level; the offense, escape risk and conduct do.
Family income and educational level
Socioeconomic status is not a basis for security classification.
Preference of the inmate and family
Inmates do not choose their security level; it is assessed from crime severity, escape risk and behavior.
Relying on the warden's personal judgment
That is subjective classification. Objective classification uses standardized, scored criteria.
Placing inmates in order of arrival
Order of arrival is not a classification method; objective systems score each inmate on set criteria.
Letting inmates choose their own housing unit
Placement is decided by the institution using standardized criteria, not by the inmates.
Assigning inmates to cells in order of arrival
Order of arrival ignores risk and needs, which are the basis of classification.
Grouping inmates by home region
Where an inmate comes from is not a classification basis; inmates are classified by risk and needs.
Ranking inmates by their length of stay
Time served alone does not classify inmates; classification weighs risk and needs.
Age, health, and physical condition
Health and age may affect housing or medical care, but security classification rests on the crime, sentence and escape risk.
Educational attainment and work skills
These guide program and work assignments, not security classification.
Financial status and family connections
Wealth or connections must never decide the security level; it is based on the crime, sentence and escape risk.
Bureau of Jail Management and Penology
BJMP runs city, district and municipal jails for detainees and short-term prisoners; it does not supervise probationers.
Bureau of Corrections
BuCor manages the national penitentiaries for inmates serving long sentences, not probationers in the community.
Board of Pardons and Parole
The Board grants parole and recommends clemency; field supervision of probationers is done by the PPA.
The Court of Appeals
Under PD 968 the application is filed with and decided by the trial court that convicted the offender, not an appellate court.
The Board of Pardons and Parole
The Board handles parole and clemency. Probation is granted by the trial court.
The President
The President grants pardon and other clemency, not probation, which is a judicial grant.
Those convicted for the first time
First offenders are the main beneficiaries of probation; being a first-time offender does not disqualify anyone.
Those sentenced to a fine only
PD 968 allows probation whether the sentence is imprisonment or a fine only, so a fine does not disqualify.
Those sentenced to exactly 6 years
The bar is a maximum term of MORE than six years. A sentence of exactly six years is still within the limit.
Rules for the parole board's hearings
Those are procedural rules of the Board. Conditions of probation bind the probationer.
Requirements to file an application
Those must be met before probation is granted. Conditions are the rules the probationer must keep while on probation.
Penalties for the probation officer
Conditions apply to the probationer, not to the officer who supervises them.
Parole and Probation Administration
The PPA supervises parolees after release, but parole itself is granted by the Board of Pardons and Parole.
The sentencing trial court
Courts grant probation, not parole. Parole is granted by the Board of Pardons and Parole.
Bureau of Corrections
BuCor holds the inmate and forwards records, but it does not grant parole.
Postponement of sentence
That is a reprieve. Commutation reduces the sentence, for example from death to life imprisonment.
Forgiveness of the offense
That is pardon. Commutation keeps the conviction but lowers the penalty.
Release on parole
Parole is release under supervision. Commutation is an act of clemency that reduces the sentence.
Permanent reduction of the sentence
That is commutation. A reprieve only delays the execution of the sentence.
Forgiveness that restores all rights
That describes an absolute pardon. A reprieve only postpones the sentence.
Early release under supervision
That is parole. A reprieve is a temporary stay of the sentence.
Delaying the penalty
That is a reprieve. Commutation actually lowers the penalty.
Erasing the conviction entirely
Commutation leaves the conviction in place and only lowers the penalty. Obliterating the offense is the effect of amnesty.
Suspending the penalty on probation
That is probation, granted by the court. Commutation is an executive act that reduces the penalty.
Judicial power to suspend a sentence
Courts may suspend a sentence through probation; clemency is the President's power under Art. VII, Sec. 19 of the Constitution.
Legislative power to define penalties
Congress defines crimes and penalties; clemency is an executive power.
Police power to release
The police cannot grant clemency; it belongs to the President.
Forgiveness subject to conditions
That is a conditional pardon. An absolute pardon carries no conditions.
General pardon for a class of offenders
That is amnesty, granted to a group, often political offenders. A pardon is given to an individual.
Reduction of the penalty imposed
That is commutation. An absolute pardon forgives the offender fully.
Pardon given to a group of offenders
That is amnesty. A conditional pardon is given to one person and binds them to conditions.
Release granted by the court before imprisonment
That is probation. A conditional pardon is executive clemency, granted by the President after conviction.
Release by the Board after serving the minimum
That is parole. A conditional pardon comes from the President, and breaking its conditions is punished under Art. 159 RPC.
Individual pardon for a common crime
That is an ordinary pardon, given to one person. Amnesty is general, usually for political offenses, with the concurrence of Congress.
Court order dismissing a criminal case
Amnesty is granted by the President with the concurrence of Congress, not by a court.
Release after serving the minimum term
That is parole. Amnesty may be granted even before trial or conviction.
The Regional Trial Court
Courts grant probation, not parole. Parole is granted by the Board of Pardons and Parole.
Parole and Probation Administration
The PPA supervises parolees once released, but the grant of parole comes from the Board.
The Secretary of Justice
The Board is attached to the DOJ, but the grant itself is made by the Board of Pardons and Parole.
Guarding inmates inside the prison
Custodial staff guard inmates in prison. Parole supervision happens outside, after release.
Reviewing applications for parole
The Board reviews applications. Supervision begins only after the parolee is released.
Monitoring probationers placed by the court
That is probation supervision. Parolees are released from prison by the Board; probationers are never imprisoned.
Changing jobs after informing the officer
Reporting a job change to the parole officer is compliance, not a violation.
Attending a required counseling program
Taking part in required programs means a condition is being met.
Finding steady employment
Holding a job is encouraged and is often one of the conditions of parole.
Release granted at the discretion of the Board
That is discretionary parole. Mandatory release happens by law once the required time is served.
Release ordered after a successful appeal
An acquittal on appeal frees the accused because the conviction falls, not because time was served.
Transfer to a lower security facility
A transfer is not a release; the inmate stays in custody.
Agency that supervises probationers in the field
That is the Parole and Probation Administration. The Board decides parole and clemency cases.
Court that hears appeals in criminal cases
Appeals go to the Court of Appeals or the Supreme Court. The Board is an executive body under the DOJ.
Bureau that runs the national penitentiaries
That is the Bureau of Corrections. The Board decides on parole and clemency.
Is granted by the court that tried the case
That describes probation. Parole is granted by the Board of Pardons and Parole.
Is granted instead of serving any prison term
That describes probation, which is granted in place of imprisonment.
Is granted only to those sentenced to 6 years or less
The six-year ceiling is a probation rule (PD 968). Parole under the Indeterminate Sentence Law applies to longer prison terms.
Searching cells for hidden contraband
That is a shakedown. A lockdown confines all inmates to their cells, often during an emergency.
Moving inmates to another facility
That is a transfer. A lockdown keeps inmates where they are, locked in their cells.
Counting inmates at set times
That is a head count. A lockdown suspends movement and confines everyone to cells.
Scheduled count of all inmates
That is a head count. A shakedown is an unannounced search for contraband.
Confining inmates to their cells
That is a lockdown. A shakedown is a search, which may happen during a lockdown.
Questioning inmates about an incident
That is an interview or investigation, not a search for contraband.
Separating inmates as a disciplinary penalty
That is disciplinary segregation, a sanction for a rule violation. Administrative segregation is not a punishment; it is for security.
Placing inmates in the general population
General population is the opposite; administrative segregation removes inmates from it.
Assigning inmates to a work detail
A work detail is a program assignment, not segregation.
Serving sentences of less than 3 years
Short terms point to minimum security, and terms of three years or less are usually served in jail rather than prison.
With good conduct and about to be released
Inmates near release with good conduct are usually minimum security.
On work-release programs
Work release is for minimum-security inmates who can be trusted outside the facility.
Committing a new crime while on probation
A new crime is a new-offense violation, not a technical one.
Failing to apply for probation on time
That bars the grant of probation. A violation can only happen after probation has been granted.
Finishing probation ahead of schedule
Completing probation is not a violation of it.
Time deduction for loyalty during a calamity
That is the Special Time Allowance for Loyalty under RA 10592, a separate credit from GCTA.
Time deduction for study and teaching
That is the Time Allowance for Study, Teaching and Mentoring under RA 10592, separate from GCTA.
Credit for preventive detention
That is the credit for preventive imprisonment under Art. 29 RPC, not GCTA.
Deterring crime through certain, swift punishment
That is deterrence. Restorative justice focuses on repairing the harm done to the victim and community.
Paying back society through proportionate punishment
That is retribution, or just deserts. Restorative justice seeks repair, not proportional suffering.
Removing offenders from society to protect the public
That is incapacitation. Restorative justice brings offender, victim and community together.
Controlling inmates through medication alone
Medication is a medical measure; behavior modification uses reinforcement and structured programs.
Punishing inmates for every rule violation
Punishment alone is not behavior modification, which relies on structured programs that reinforce desired behavior.
Isolating inmates until they comply
Isolation is segregation, not a treatment program.
Inmates work only inside the prison
Prison industries keep inmates inside. Work release lets them work in the community and return at night.
Inmates are paroled to work
Parole is release from prison. On work release the inmate is still serving the sentence and returns to the facility.
Inmates train for jobs after release
That is vocational training. Work release means actual work outside during the day.
Treating dependence on alcohol and drugs
That is substance abuse treatment. Anger management teaches inmates to control aggression.
Teaching job skills for after release
That is vocational training, not anger management.
Isolating inmates who start fights
That is disciplinary segregation, a sanction, not a treatment program.
Work-based program outside the prison
That describes work release. A therapeutic community is a live-in treatment community.
Unit for inmates under discipline
That is disciplinary segregation, a sanction, not treatment.
Classification unit for new inmates
That is the reception and diagnostic center.
Step-by-step inmate classification system
Classification is done by the reception and diagnostic center; the 12 steps are the Alcoholics Anonymous recovery model.
Graduated system of disciplinary penalties
Disciplinary penalties are not the 12 steps, which come from Alcoholics Anonymous.
Reentry plan for parolees
A reentry plan prepares an inmate for release. The 12 steps are a recovery model for addiction.
Discipline through strict isolation
A therapeutic community works through a community of peers, not isolation.
Job placement through outside employers
That is work release or reentry. A TC focuses on recovery from drug dependence through peer support.
Education through formal school classes
That is the education program. A TC is a self-help community model for drug rehabilitation.
